parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Define electric potential at a point.

markscheme_points.text: work done (on charge) in moving positive charge from infinity (to the point)

hints: Hint 1: Think about what potential really measures - it is energy per unit of something, so what charge do you consider moving to test the field?
Hint 2: Remember where we define potential to be zero, and complete the idea by stating the start and end points of the movement.
parts.proper_answer: Electric potential at a point is the work done per unit charge in moving a small positive charge from infinity to the point.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Potential Means Energy Per Charge**
Think of electric potential $V$ as telling you how much potential energy each coulomb of charge would have at that point. So you always divide work done $W$ by the test charge $q$: $$V = \frac{W}{q}$$

Step 2: **Fix The Reference And The Test Charge**
By agreement $V = 0$ at infinity where there is no field. To make the definition standard we always use a small positive test charge, moved from infinity to the point. That gives the full 2-mark definition.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem:
An isolated conducting sphere is charged. Fig. 5.1 shows the variation of the potential $V$ due to the sphere with displacement $x$ from its centre.

{{figure:figure_5_1}}

Fig. 5.1

Use Fig. 5.1 to determine:
hints: Hint 1: Look closely at the shape in Fig. 5.1 - where is $V$ flat and constant, and where does it start to curve as $1/x$? What does that boundary tell you about the surface?
parts.proper_answer: Radius is where constant $V$ ends, at $x = 0.060\text{ m}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Inside Versus Outside A Conductor**
Inside an isolated conducting sphere charge sits on the surface, so there is no field inside and $V$ is constant everywhere up to the surface. Outside, the sphere acts like a point charge at the centre, so $$V = \frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 x}$$ which falls in magnitude as $1/x$.

Step 2: **Read The Changeover From The Graph**
In Fig. 5.1 the flat section is from $x = 0$ to about $x = 0.06\text{ m}$ on both sides, then the curve begins. That changeover is the surface. So $$r = 0.060\text{ m}$$

parts.label: (b)(ii)

markscheme_points.text: V = Q / 4πε0x; Q = (−) 850 × 4π × 8.85 × 10⁻¹² × 0.060 or Q = (−) 850 × 0.060 / 8.99 × 10⁹ (any correct pair of V and x values from curve)

hints: Hint 1: Outside the sphere the potential follows the point-charge law, so pick any clear $(x,V)$ pair on the curved part of the graph, for example at the surface.
Hint 2: Rearrange $V = Q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0 x)$ for $Q$ and check the sign - negative $V$ must mean negative $Q$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Apply The Point-Charge Formula Outside**
For $x$ greater than the radius: $$V = \frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 x}$$ so $$Q = 4\pi\varepsilon_0 x V$$ Pick a reliable point. At the surface $x = 0.060\text{ m}$, $V = -850\text{ V}$ from the graph. Any other curved-section pair works the same.

Step 2: **Substitute And Keep The Sign**
$$Q = 4\pi \times 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times 0.060 \times (-850)$$ $$Q \approx -5.7 \times 10^{-9}\text{ C}$$ The negative sign is essential because $V$ is negative everywhere, showing the sphere is negatively charged.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.part_stem:
Two spheres are identical to the sphere in (b). Each sphere has the same charge as the sphere in (b).

The spheres are held in a vacuum so that their centres are separated by a distance of $0.46\text{ m}$. Assume that the charge on each sphere is a point charge at the centre of the sphere.
parts.text: Calculate the electric potential energy $E_{\text{P}}$ of the two spheres.
hints: Hint 1: Think of $E_P$ as the work to bring one charge from infinity into the potential due to the other charge, so which product of charges and separation matters here?
Hint 2: Use the magnitude of $Q$ from (b)(ii) with separation $r = 0.46\text{ m}$ and calculate $Q^2/(4\pi\varepsilon_0 r)$ carefully with powers of ten.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Energy Of A Pair**
Potential energy of two point charges $Q$ separated by $r$ is charge times potential: $$E_P = \frac{Q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$$ Here $Q = 5.67 \times 10^{-9}\text{ C}$ on each sphere and $r = 0.46\text{ m}$. The square makes $E_P$ positive even though $Q$ is negative.

Step 2: **Calculate**
$$E_P = \frac{(5.67 \times 10^{-9})^2}{4\pi \times 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times 0.46}$$ $$E_P \approx 6.3 \times 10^{-7}\text{ J}$$ This is the work that was done to hold them this close together.

key_concepts: electric potential energy of two point charges
hints: Hint 1: Think of $E_P$ as the work to bring one charge from infinity into the potential due to the other charge, so which product of charges and separation matters here?
Hint 2: Use the magnitude of $Q$ from (b)(ii) with separation $r = 0.46\text{ m}$ and calculate $Q^2/(4\pi\varepsilon_0 r)$ carefully with powers of ten.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text:
The two spheres are now released simultaneously so that they are free to move.

Describe and explain the subsequent motion of the spheres.

markscheme_points.text: force is repulsive so spheres move apart; force in direction of motion so speed increases; potential energy converted to kinetic energy so speed increases; force decreases with distance so acceleration decreases; momentum is conserved (at zero) (and masses are equal) so velocities are always equal and opposite

hints: Hint 1: Start with the sign of the charges - do like charges attract or repel, and which way does the resulting force point relative to the motion?
Hint 2: Think about energy - as separation grows, what happens to $E_P$ and where does that lost energy go?
Hint 3: Think about how force varies with distance, and with equal masses starting from rest, how the two velocities must compare to keep total momentum zero.
parts.proper_answer: Spheres repel and move apart with increasing speed as $E_P$ is converted to kinetic energy. Acceleration decreases as force falls with distance. Speeds remain equal and opposite by conservation of momentum.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Repulsion Drives Them Apart**
Both charges are negative so the Coulomb force is repulsive. On release each sphere is pushed away from the other, so force is in the direction of motion and each sphere speeds up from rest.

Step 2: **Energy Change And Falling Acceleration**
As $r$ increases, $E_P = Q^2/4\pi\varepsilon_0 r$ decreases and that loss appears as kinetic energy, so speed increases. But $F \propto 1/r^2$, so force and hence acceleration $a = F/m$ get smaller with distance. Motion is accelerating apart with decreasing acceleration.

Step 3: **Symmetry From Momentum**
Initially total momentum is zero and no external force acts. With identical masses the spheres must always have equal and opposite velocities to keep total momentum zero, so their motions are mirror images.
